name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
description: A nearly complete skull found in 2001 in the Djurab Desert of Chad, nicknamed Toumaï, is about seven million years old, close to the time our lineage split from that of chimpanzees. Its brain was no bigger than a chimpanzee's, but its canine teeth were small and the opening for the spinal cord sat further under the skull, hinting that it may have walked upright. Found 2,500 kilometres west of the East African Rift, it showed that the earliest hominins lived across a much wider part of Africa than once thought.

name: Homo habilis
description: Named in 1964 from fossils at Olduvai Gorge, Homo habilis, the 'handy man', was long thought to be the first maker of stone tools. It lived in East Africa between roughly 2.5 and 1.6 million years ago, with a brain somewhat larger than the australopiths', smaller teeth, and hands capable of a precise grip. Older tools from Lomekwi show that toolmaking began before it, and its place in our genus is still argued over, but it marks the first steps of Homo.

Makers of Acheulean handaxes, they reached China and Java and survived for nearly two million years, the last of them on Java around 110,000 years ago.

Proteins from its tooth enamel suggest it was a close relative of the lineage that later gave rise to Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans.

name: Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthal)

At the Sima de los Huesos in Spain, a pit holding at least 28 individuals about 430,000 years old shows their lineage already taking shape. They made Mousterian stone tools, controlled fire, hunted large game and buried some of their dead. They disappeared around 40,000 years ago, but most people living outside Africa today carry a little Neanderthal DNA.

Together with finds such as Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, they suggest Homo sapiens took shape across many parts of Africa rather than in one place. name: Denisovans
description: Denisovans were the first human group discovered through DNA alone. In 2010 the genome from a tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave, in Siberia's Altai Mountains, turned out to belong to an unknown population, related to but distinct from Neanderthals. Since then a jaw from the Tibetan Plateau and a skull from Harbin in China have been identified as Denisovan. They interbred with Neanderthals and with modern humans: people in Papua New Guinea and Australia carry several percent Denisovan DNA, and Tibetans owe a gene for life at high altitude to them.

name: Homo floresiensis
description: On the Indonesian island of Flores, a team excavating Liang Bua cave in 2003 found the skeleton of a tiny adult woman, about a metre tall, with a brain no bigger than a chimpanzee's. Nicknamed the Hobbit, Homo floresiensis lived there until about 60,000 years ago, hunting dwarf elephants called Stegodon alongside Komodo dragons. Older finds on the island suggest its ancestors arrived around a million years ago and shrank over time, as island animals often do.

name: Middle Stone Age (Africa)
description: In Africa the long age after the handaxes is called the Middle Stone Age, beginning around 300,000 years ago alongside the first Homo sapiens. Its people struck flakes from carefully prepared cores and made stone spear points, and at Pinnacle Point on South Africa's south coast, some 164,000 years ago, they were already gathering shellfish and grinding red ochre. Later sites such as Blombos Cave and Diepkloof add engraved ochre, shell beads and decorated ostrich eggshell, early signs of symbolic thought.

name: Levallois / Mousterian
description: The Mousterian is the toolkit of the Neanderthals, named after the rock shelter of Le Moustier in France. Its makers shaped a stone core with care so that a single blow would strike off a flake of planned size and shape, a method known as Levallois, then retouched the flakes into scrapers and points. With these tools Neanderthals hunted reindeer, horse and bison across Europe and western Asia for some 200,000 years, and at Pech de l'Azé in France they left blocks of manganese that may have helped them light fires.

name: Châtelperronian
description: The Châtelperronian, named after a cave at Châtelperron in central France, appeared around 44,000 years ago, just as modern humans were entering Europe. Its makers produced curved-backed stone knives and, at the Grotte du Renne at Arcy-sur-Cure, pierced animal teeth and bone ornaments. Neanderthal remains found with it at Saint-Césaire and Arcy suggest it was the work of some of the last Neanderthals, perhaps influenced by their new neighbours, though who made it is still argued over.

name: Aurignacian
description: The Aurignacian marks the arrival of modern humans across Europe from about 43,000 years ago, while Neanderthals still lived there. Its makers struck long, thin stone blades, shaped spear points from bone and antler, and wore beads of shell, ivory and animal teeth. In the caves of the Swabian Jura they carved the oldest known figurines, among them the Lion Man and the Venus of Hohle Fels, and played flutes of bird bone and mammoth ivory; the paintings of Chauvet Cave in France belong to the same world.

name: Gravettian
description: From roughly 35,000 years ago the Gravettian spread from the Atlantic coast to the Russian plains, as the climate slid towards the coldest stretch of the Ice Age. Its people hunted mammoth, and on the plains built huts framed with mammoth bones. They are best known for small carved 'Venus' figurines such as the Venus of Willendorf, and at Dolní Věstonice in Moravia they fired figures of clay in hearths more than 26,000 years ago, long before anyone made pottery vessels. Some of their dead were buried with rich ornaments.

name: Solutrean
description: As the ice sheets neared their greatest extent, between about 24,000 and 17,000 years ago, people in France and Spain developed the Solutrean, named after the great rock of Solutré in Burgundy. Its makers mastered pressure flaking, pressing tiny flakes off a stone blank with a pointed bone tool to make thin, symmetrical 'laurel leaf' points, some too fine to have been used for hunting. At Parpalló in Spain they left thousands of small stone slabs engraved and painted with animals.

name: Epigravettian
description: While the ice sheets were at their greatest, about twenty thousand years ago, people held on in the warmer south and east of Europe: in Italy, the Balkans and the plains of Ukraine. Their way of life, the Epigravettian, followed the Gravettian and lasted until the end of the Ice Age. They set tiny flint blades into their spears to hunt horse, ibex and bison, and on the Ukrainian plains some built huts framed with mammoth bones. Genetic studies suggest that as the climate warmed, people related to them spread north across the continent.

name: Magdalenian
description: The Magdalenian, named after the rock shelter of La Madeleine in France, was the last great culture of the Ice Age in western Europe, from about 17,000 to 11,000 years ago. Its people followed herds of reindeer and horse, hurled spears with carved spear-throwers and fished with barbed antler harpoons. They painted the ceiling of Altamira in Spain and decorated many other caves, and carved lifelike animals into bone and antler. As the climate warmed and the reindeer moved north, their way of life gave way to new ones.

name: Natufian
description: In the oak woodlands of the Levant, about fifteen thousand years ago, the Natufians began to stay in one place all year round. At Ain Mallaha, in the upper Jordan valley, they built round houses on stone footings and buried their dead beneath the floors; one elderly person was laid to rest with a hand on a puppy. They cut wild wheat and barley with flint sickles and ground them in stone mortars, and in Jordan they baked the oldest known bread. When the cold of the Younger Dryas returned, many researchers think it pushed their descendants towards farming.

Clovis was long thought to mark the first Americans, but older sites such as Monte Verde in Chile show people had arrived thousands of years before.

name: Maglemosian culture
description: When the ice had gone, Britain was not yet an island. At Star Carr in Yorkshire they built wooden platforms at a lake's edge and wore headdresses made from the skulls and antlers of red deer. As the sea rose the plain shrank, until by about eight thousand years ago it had drowned beneath the North Sea, where fishing boats still dredge up their tools.

description: Around 5500 BCE farming reached the heart of Europe. name: Ertebølle culture

At the type site on the Limfjord they left a great mound of oyster and mussel shells, and at Tybrind Vig their dugout canoes and carved paddles survive under the sea. description: Most of the languages spoken across Africa south of the equator are close relatives, the Bantu languages, because their speakers' ancestors spread out from one small homeland: the highlands between Cameroon and Nigeria. Over three thousand years farming villages moved south along the rivers and coasts of the rainforest and east around its northern edge. By about 500 BCE the eastern stream had reached Lake Victoria, where the Urewe culture made dimpled pottery and smelted iron, and by around 300 CE farmers had reached South Africa. Genomes show they mixed with the foragers and herders already living there.

name: Corded Ware culture
description: Across northern and central Europe, from the Rhine to the Volga, people of the Corded Ware culture buried their dead singly under round mounds, men lying on their right side and women on their left, with pots decorated by pressing cord into the wet clay. Ancient DNA from these graves shows a sudden change: about three quarters of their ancestry came from the steppe herders of the east, mixed with that of Europe's earlier farmers. Most of their men carried the father's line R1a.

name: Bell Beaker culture
description: The Bell Beaker culture is named after its drinking cups, shaped like an upturned bell, found in graves from Portugal to Hungary and from Sicily to Scotland. It probably began in Iberia, but in central Europe it was taken up by people of steppe descent. When they reached Britain, around 2450 BCE, about nine tenths of the island's ancestry was replaced within a few centuries. The Amesbury Archer, buried near Stonehenge with gold ornaments and copper knives, had grown up in the Alps.

name: Únětice culture
description: In the heart of central Europe, from Bohemia and Saxony to western Poland, the Únětice culture of the Early Bronze Age grew rich on bronze and on trade in amber and salt. Its rulers were buried under great mounds such as Leubingen, with gold and bronze weapons, and the Nebra sky disc, the oldest known picture of the night sky, comes from its world. Its people descended from both the Corded Ware and the Bell Beaker groups: steppe ancestry, now settled in the middle of Europe.

name: Sintashta culture
description: In the southern Urals, around four thousand years ago, the Sintashta culture built fortified settlements ringed by walls and ditches, and mined and worked copper on a scale unusual for steppe peoples. In its graves lie the oldest known chariots, light two-wheeled vehicles with spoked wheels, buried with their horses. Ancient DNA shows its people descended largely from the Corded Ware groups of eastern Europe, and many researchers see them as early speakers of the Indo-Iranian languages.

name: Andronovo culture
description: From the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei in Siberia, and south into Central Asia, the Andronovo culture spread a way of life built on cattle, horses and bronze across the steppe in the second millennium BCE. Its people buried their dead crouched in stone-lined graves with richly decorated pottery. Closely related to the Sintashta people before them, they carried steppe ancestry deep into Asia, and scholars agree they spoke Indo-Iranian languages, the family that later gave us Sanskrit and Persian.

name: Lapita culture
description: Around 3,500 years ago a seafaring people appeared suddenly in the Bismarck Archipelago north of New Guinea, making red pottery stamped with fine toothed patterns. Within a few centuries their outrigger canoes had carried them thousands of kilometres east, to islands no one had ever reached: Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, and by about 900 BCE Tonga and Samoa. They took pigs, dogs and chickens with them, and taro, yams, bananas and breadfruit to plant. Their ancestors came from Taiwan and the northern Philippines, and their descendants became the Polynesians.

name: Sumerian City-States
description: In the river plains of southern Mesopotamia, cities such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash grew in the late fourth millennium BCE into the world's first urban civilization. Sumerian scribes invented cuneiform writing on clay tablets, temple communities raised stepped ziggurats, and canals turned the dry plain into rich farmland. The city-states fought one another over water and land for centuries, fell under Akkadian and later Babylonian rule, and by about 1750 BCE had lost their independence, though their language lived on in temples and schools.

His grandson Naram-Sin called himself king of the four quarters of the world and was worshipped as a god. Within two centuries the empire had collapsed, weakened by revolts, by raids from the Zagros mountains and, many believe, by a severe drought.

Thousands of clay tablets from their archives preserve the oldest written Indo-European language. Around 1180 BCE the empire collapsed and Hattusa was abandoned, in the wider upheaval at the end of the Bronze Age.

name: Cai
description: An ancient Chinese vassal state founded in the 11th century BCE by a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou in modern Henan. name: Cao
description: A regional vassal state of the Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods, established in the 11th century BCE in modern western Shandong. name: Chen
description: An ancient Zhou vassal state situated in modern eastern Henan, traditionally founded by Duke Hu as descendants of the legendary sage-king Shun. name: Chu
description: A major southern powerhouse along the Yangtze and Han river valleys during the Zhou dynasty, with its capital at Ying in modern Hubei. name: Jin
description: The dominant northern super-state of the Spring and Autumn period, occupying modern Shanxi and northern Henan. name: Later Zhou
description: The Eastern Zhou dynasty (770–256 BCE), established when King Ping moved the royal capital east to Luoyang following nomadic Rong raids that destroyed the western capital. Though royal power declined to nominal ceremonial status, this era witnessed immense intellectual flowering during the Hundred Schools of Thought, including Confucianism and Daoism.

name: Lu
description: An influential Zhou vassal state in modern Shandong, founded by Boqin, the son of the revered Duke of Zhou. Celebrated as the cultural heartland of classical ritual, historical chronicle keeping, and moral philosophy, Lu was the birthplace of Confucius, preserving ancient Zhou rites long after other states had abandoned them.

name: Qi
description: A wealthy and powerful maritime state in modern Shandong, founded in the 11th century BCE for the grand strategist Jiang Ziya. Blessed with rich coastal sea salt and silk industries, Qi established early hegemony under Duke Huan and prime minister Guan Zhong, later founding the renowned Jixia Academy of scholarly debate.

media.title: Qi State: An Important Vassal State in Pre-Qin Period

name: Qin
description: A rugged frontier state in the western Wei River valley of modern Shaanxi, traditionally tasked with breeding warhorses and defending Zhou frontiers against nomadic tribes. Implementing radical Legalist reforms under Shang Yang, Qin developed a meritocratic military and centralized bureaucracy that ultimately conquered all rival states to unify China in 221 BCE.

name: Roman Kingdom
description: The foundational monarchical period of ancient Rome, traditionally inaugurated by Romulus in 753 BCE and ending with the expulsion of the tyrant Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE. During this era, Rome evolved from a modest pastoral settlement on the Tiber into an organized city-state, establishing the Senate, curiae, and core religious institutions.

name: Song
description: An ancient central plains state in modern eastern Henan, granted by the Zhou kings to the surviving royal nobility of the defeated Shang dynasty to maintain ancestral rites. name: Teng
description: A minor aristocratic vassal state situated in modern southern Shandong during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. name: Wey
description: A resilient central plains state along the Yellow River in modern northern Henan, founded by Kangshu, a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou. Renowned for poetry preserved in the Book of Songs and commercial craftsmanship, Wey survived as a small buffer state longer than any other, persisting until Qin annexation in 209 BCE.

media.title: The Western Zhou Dynasty and the Spring and Autumn Period - Explained

name: Wu
description: A dynamic maritime and riverine kingdom in the lower Yangtze delta of modern Jiangsu, centered around modern Suzhou. Expanding rapidly in the late Spring and Autumn period with the strategic advice of Sun Tzu, Wu dominated regional waterways with specialized navies and prized cast-bronze swords before being conquered by neighboring Yue in 473 BCE.

name: Xu
description: An ancient non-Zhou Huaiyi confederation and state based along the Huai River valley in modern Anhui and Jiangsu. name: Yan
description: A major northeastern frontier kingdom centered at modern Beijing, established at the start of the Western Zhou dynasty by the Duke of Shao. name: Zheng
description: An influential central plains vassal state founded in the late Western Zhou in modern Henan, centered on the commercial capital of Xinzheng. description: Around seven million years ago, the ancestral lineage leading to humans diverged from the lineage leading to chimpanzees. name: The Laetoli footprints
description: At Laetoli in northern Tanzania, Mary Leakey's team uncovered a 27-metre trail of about seventy footprints left in wet volcanic ash some 3.7 million years ago and cemented by soft rain. Made by three individuals walking upright, generally thought to be Australopithecus afarensis, and joined by a second trackway found nearby in 2015, the prints show an arched sole, a heel-to-toe stride and a big toe in line with the rest of the foot, proving that our ancestors walked much like us long before brains grew large or the first stone tools were struck.

name: Earliest stone tools (Lomekwian)
description: Archaeologists working at the Lomekwi 3 site discovered the oldest known intentionally flaked stone implements, pushing tool manufacture hundreds of thousands of years earlier than previously assumed. These massive basalt cores and anvils demonstrate deliberate block-on-block percussion used to crack hard plant foods or bone, proving that stone tool knapping predated the emergence of the genus Homo.

name: Systematic Oldowan flake tools
description: The Oldowan tradition marked the onset of standardized, systematically produced lithic reduction. Hominins deliberately struck river cobbles with hammerstones to produce sharp-edged flakes and chopper cores, giving our ancestors the butchery tools required to cut tough hides, strip meat from scavenged carcasses, and access lipid-dense bone marrow.

name: Early hominin expansion out of Africa (Dmanisi)
description: Excavations at Dmanisi in the southern Caucasus recovered remarkably complete crania, postcranial remains, and Oldowan stone tools dating to 1.8 million years ago. Representing the earliest undisputed record of hominins outside Africa, these small-bodied, relatively small-brained individuals prove that our ancestors ventured into Eurasia long before the emergence of tall body proportions and advanced Acheulean biface technology.

name: Acheulean handaxe technology
description: The Acheulean techno-complex introduced symmetrical, bifacially flaked teardrop handaxes, picks, and cleavers, demanding significant cognitive foresight and mental template mapping compared to earlier flake tools. This versatile toolkit spread across Africa, western Europe, and southern Asia, serving as the dominant hominin tool form for well over one million years.

name: First controlled use of fire
date_text: c. 1 million years ago (evidence at the site may reach 1.79 million)
description: Microscopic analysis of burned bone fragments and plant ashing deep within Wonderwerk Cave confirms that hominins were deliberately managing fire in enclosed shelters by one million years ago. Regular access to fire dramatically lowered digestion costs through cooking, expanded available dietary calories, offered nocturnal defense against apex predators, and lengthened social contact hours after dark.

name: Earliest wooden structure
description: Wood rarely survives in the ground, so the Stone Age is named after the stones it left behind. Yet in waterlogged riverbank sediments at Kalambo Falls in Zambia, excavators uncovered two logs of large-fruited bushwillow shaped with stone tools and joined at right angles by a carved U-shaped notch, dated by luminescence to about 476,000 years ago. Found alongside a wooden wedge, a digging stick and Acheulean stone tools, the interlocking logs probably formed a raised walkway or platform above the wet floodplain long before Homo sapiens appeared.

name: Wooden hunting spears at Schöningen
date_text: c. 337,000–300,000 years ago (estimates from 400,000 to 200,000 years ago have been proposed)
description: In the waterlogged lakeshore sediments of an open-cast coal mine at Schöningen in northern Germany, archaeologists uncovered ten wooden spears and double-pointed throwing sticks alongside stone tools and thousands of butchered wild horse bones. Carved from slow-growing spruce and pine between about 337,000 and 300,000 years ago, the spears are tapered at both ends with their weight balanced in the front third like a modern javelin, proving that Homo heidelbergensis or early Neanderthals were skilled, cooperative big-game hunters.

name: Emergence of anatomically modern humans
description: Cranial and dental remains excavated alongside Middle Stone Age tools at Jebel Irhoud pushed the physical origin of our own species back past 300,000 years. These fossils exhibit modern facial morphologies paired with more archaic, elongated braincases, suggesting that modern humans emerged across Africa as a whole rather than in a single local cradle.

name: First intentional burials
description: At Skhul Cave on Mount Carmel and Qafzeh Cave near Nazareth in the Levant, early modern humans buried their dead in shallow pits dug into the cave floor and terrace between about 120,000 and 90,000 years ago. Alongside the flexed skeletons lay deliberate grave goods: a wild boar jaw placed on the chest of Skhul 5, red deer antlers clasped to the chest of an adolescent at Qafzeh, lumps of red ochre, and perforated marine shells carried from the Mediterranean coast. Neanderthals also buried their dead at cave sites across Eurasia, including Shanidar Cave in Iraq.

name: Early symbolic and decorative culture
description: Excavations at Blombos Cave recovered smoothed red ochre plaques engraved with cross-hatched geometric patterns, deliberate shell beads pierced for suspension, and dedicated pigment-processing abalone kits. These artifacts constitute some of the earliest conclusive archaeological evidence of modern human symbolic thought, non-verbal communication, and distinct personal ornamentation.

name: Invention of the bow and arrow
description: Small stone microliths and bone points from Sibudu Cave in South Africa, dating to around 64,000 years ago, show micro-wear impact damage consistent with high-velocity arrow propulsion, while perforated bone arrowheads from Fa-Hien Cave in Sri Lanka reveal that hunter-gatherers were using bows and arrows to hunt monkeys in dense tropical canopy by 48,000 years ago. Propelling light, sharpened projectiles with elastic energy transformed hunting efficiency, allowing hunters to strike elusive prey from safe distances and expanding human subsistence across varied global ecosystems.

name: Archaic admixture with Neanderthals and Denisovans
description: Genomic sequencing of fossil specimens and contemporary populations revealed that modern humans repeatedly interbred with archaic hominin lineages as they expanded across Eurasia. Initial encounters with Neanderthals introduced genetic variants present across all present-day non-African populations, while pulses of Denisovan introgression provided vital immune and high-altitude adaptations to ancestral Oceanic and East Asian groups.

name: Seafaring to Sahul
date_text: 65,000–50,000 years ago (the earliest dates are debated)
description: Modern human populations crossed Wallacea by watercraft to reach the Pleistocene continent of Sahul, joined Australia and New Guinea, with early cultural deposits at the Madjedbebe rockshelter. Because Sahul stayed separated from Asia by deep ocean channels throughout the Pleistocene, reaching it required intentional, multi-stage open-water voyaging and planned maritime exploration.

name: Eyed needles and tailored clothing
description: In the deep stratified deposits of Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains, archaeologists unearthed a seven-centimetre eyed sewing needle carved from bird bone, dating to roughly 50,000 years ago. Polished bone needles with drilled eyes also appear in Aurignacian contexts across Europe, such as Potok Cave in Slovenia. Unlike simple bone awls that pierced hides for coarse lacing, fine eyed needles allowed multiple layers of animal furs, skins, and textiles to be tightly stitched with sinew thread into windproof, form-fitting garments and footwear, a technological breakthrough that enabled human survival in sub-zero Ice Age climates.

description: Uranium-series dating of calcite crusts overlaying cave wall paintings at Leang Karampuang identified representational art showing human-like figures interacting with a wild pig. This find predates the famous cave art sites of western Europe, showing that narrative painting and visual storytelling were established long before the Last Glacial Maximum.

name: Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions
description: The close of the Pleistocene epoch witnessed the catastrophic collapse of the world's megafauna, with over two-thirds of all large mammal species vanishing from the Earth. In the Americas and Australia, where native species had never encountered hominin hunters, extinction rates exceeded eighty percent, claiming mammoth, mastodon, sabre-toothed cats, dire wolves, and giant ground sloths in rapid ecological succession. Driven by a devastating combination of human hunting, landscape fire alteration, and rapid post-glacial climatic change, the loss of these ecosystem engineers fundamentally reshaped global biomes.

name: Extinction of the Neanderthals
description: After inhabiting Eurasia for hundreds of thousands of years, the Neanderthals disappeared from the fossil record around 40,000 years ago. High-precision radiocarbon dating across dozens of European cave sites reveals that Mousterian stone tool industries were replaced by Upper Paleolithic technologies within a narrow window between 41,000 and 39,000 years ago. While small refugial populations may have lingered on the southern margins of Iberia at sites like Gorham's Cave, competitive pressure from expanding modern humans, sudden climatic volatility, and progressive genetic absorption brought an end to our closest evolutionary kin.

Featuring precisely spaced finger holes designed for acoustic scales, these instruments show that complex auditory art, shared performance, and ritual music accompanied the symbolic flowering of early modern humans in Europe.

name: Peopling of the Americas
description: Fossilized human trackways at White Sands confirm modern humans walked the interior of North America during the Last Glacial Maximum, while early foraging campsites at Monte Verde establish human settlement in southern South America before 14,000 years ago. These pre-Clovis discoveries decisively overturned the "Clovis First" model, confirming that ancestral indigenous populations dispersed across the Western Hemisphere thousands of years earlier than once believed.

name: Invention of pottery
description: Radiocarbon dates from Xianrendong Cave confirmed that hunter-gatherer bands manufactured fire-hardened ceramic vessels thousands of years before the advent of agriculture. These early pots enabled mobile foragers to boil tough wild seeds, extract bone greases, process freshwater mollusks, and cook stews in durable, flame-tolerant containers.

description: Genetic and skeletal evidence shows that Eurasian gray wolf populations integrated into human hunter-gatherer camps toward the end of the Pleistocene, becoming our first animal domesticates. Joint burials, such as the Bonn–Oberkassel grave holding two humans and a cared-for puppy, highlight their integration into human foraging, sentry duty, and social structures.

description: Hunter-gatherers in Southwest Asia began selecting and cultivating founder crops, including emmer wheat, einkorn, barley and lentils, alongside domesticating sheep and goats. This transition from foraging to food production drove permanent village life, food surpluses, land tenure, and substantial regional population growth.

name: Monumental architecture at Göbekli Tepe
description: Göbekli Tepe features concentric circles of massive T-shaped limestone megaliths decorated with high-relief carvings of predators, snakes, and wild boars. Built before the invention of pottery, metal, or settled farming, the site shows that cooperative ritual and monumental construction helped catalyze sedentary communal lifestyles.

name: Squash and maize in Mesoamerica
description: In the dry hills of Oaxaca in southern Mexico, people sheltering in Guilá Naquitz Cave were growing squash more than 10,000 years ago, the earliest known crop in the Americas. Maize took longer. It was bred from teosinte, a wild grass, about 9,000 years ago, most likely in the valley of the Balsas River, and from that single beginning it spread across the Americas. Planted with beans and squash, the Three Sisters, it became the staple of the Americas' farmers.

name: Domestication of cattle and pigs
description: Around 10,500 years ago, farmers in the upper Tigris and Euphrates valleys began breeding the animals they had long hunted. Wild aurochs were slowly turned into smaller, tamer herds of cattle, and wild boar became the first pigs. At Çayönü in southeastern Turkey, one of the places where pigs may first have been domesticated, the bones show cattle managed for centuries before they grew any smaller. Pigs were domesticated a second time, separately, in China about 8,000 years ago.

name: Potatoes and llamas in the Andes
description: Around Lake Titicaca, high in the Andes of southern Peru and Bolivia, farmers domesticated the potato from a wild species between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. On the high grasslands, herders tamed the wild camelids around 6,000 to 7,000 years ago: the guanaco became the llama, a pack animal, and the vicuña the alpaca, kept for its fine wool. Guinea pigs were domesticated in the Andes too. Together they became the foundations of Andean life, up to the time of the Inca.

name: Rice and millet in China
description: China was one of the places where farming began on its own. In the north, on the foothills of the Taihang Mountains, people of the Cishan culture were growing broomcorn millet perhaps 10,000 years ago, and stored it in deep pits that could hold a tonne. To the south, rice was domesticated from wild rice in the Yangtze River basin about 9,000 years ago. At Jiahu, between the two, villagers grew both, and brewed a drink from rice, honey and hawthorn.

date_text: c. 9,000 years ago (drainage ditches); bananas 6,900–6,400 years ago
description: High in the mountains of New Guinea, at Kuk Swamp, people began digging ditches to drain the wetland about 9,000 years ago, turning it into garden land for taro. Later, between 6,900 and 6,400 years ago, they planted bananas and sugar cane. New Guinea's farmers learned from no one: it is one of the few places in the world where agriculture was invented independently, and Kuk has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.

name: The first milk
description: Animals were first kept for meat, but within a few thousand years farmers had learned to milk them. Traces of milk fat soaked into the walls of cooking pots show that people in northwestern Anatolia were milking their herds by the seventh millennium BCE. Dairying spread with farming into Europe, where clay sieves for making cheese appear in Kuyavia, in Poland, by 5500 BCE. Over the following millennia a genetic change that lets adults digest milk became common among Europeans.

name: Chinchorro artificial mummification
description: In the hyper-arid coastal desert of northern Chile and southern Peru, the Chinchorro hunter-gatherer-fishers developed the earliest known artificial mummification in human history, predating Egyptian mummies by over two millennia. Mortuary artisans carefully removed internal organs, reinforced skeletal structures with wooden sticks and totora reeds, modeled fine clay paste over the body, and sculpted serene portrait masks painted with black manganese or red ochre and fitted with natural human hair wigs. Mummification was practiced across all ages and social ranks, keeping deceased ancestors as physical, enduring members of the community.

name: Extractive metallurgy and smelting
description: Early European and Near Eastern societies moved from hammering native copper to reducing copper ores in high-temperature kilns. Extracting molten copper from mineral ores laid the foundation for kiln engineering and for the later alloying with tin and arsenic that launched the Bronze Age.

name: Domestication of the horse
description: On the steppes of Kazakhstan, people of the Botai culture kept great numbers of horses around 3500 BCE, and even milked them, but DNA shows their horses were the ancestors of Przewalski's horse, not of ours. Today's domestic horses descend from a population bred around 2200 BCE in the Volga–Don region of southern Russia. Pulling light chariots with spoked wheels and carrying riders, these horses soon spread across Eurasia, changing travel, trade and war.

name: Invention of the wheel
description: The wheel-and-axle mechanism emerged in both potters' turntables and heavy four-wheeled carts across the Eurasian steppes and Mesopotamian floodplains. Replacing dragging sledges with wheeled draft wagons transformed overland cargo transport, agrarian efficiency, and regional military organization.

name: Sorghum and pearl millet in Africa
description: Africa domesticated crops of its own. Sorghum was bred from a wild grass in eastern Sudan, between the Atbara and Gash rivers, more than 5,000 years ago; grains from a site near Kassala date to 3500–3000 BCE. Pearl millet followed in the Sahel of West Africa, grown in northern Mali by 2500–2000 BCE and later at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania. Most sorghum tolerates heat and drought, and both crops later spread to India, where they are still grown.

name: The Bronze Age and bronze metallurgy
description: Metallurgists discovered that smelting copper alongside tin or arsenic produced bronze, an alloy far harder and more durable than pure copper that melted at lower temperatures and cast cleanly. This breakthrough spurred long-distance maritime and overland trade networks to secure rare tin deposits across Eurasia and the Mediterranean, establishing complex merchant routes and elite-led palatial states.

description: Cuneiform script evolved from clay tokens and administrative seals used to track grain stores, livestock and trade in growing city-states. This system of marks moved from basic pictograms to an abstract logosyllabic script, marking the beginning of recorded history, legal codification, and literature.

name: Sacred City of Caral
description: Flourishing along the arid Pacific river valleys of central coastal Peru, Caral is the oldest known civilization and urban center in the Americas, developing monumental stepped platform pyramids and sunken circular plazas contemporary with Egypt's Old Kingdom. Sustained by maritime trade exchanging anchovies and mollusks from the coast for cotton and squash irrigated from the Supe River, Caral lacked defensive fortifications or signs of warfare, instead organizing complex regional labor through shared religious ritual, music played on carved pelican-bone flutes, and recording systems including early knotted quipu strings.

description: Built as the tomb of Pharaoh Khufu during Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for over 3,800 years. Its construction required quarrying, transporting and aligning roughly 2.3 million multi-ton limestone and granite blocks with precise astronomical orientation, reflecting state-level logistics and labour mobilization without iron tools.

name: Planned cities and sanitation in the Indus Valley
description: The Indus Valley Civilization built cities from standardized baked bricks laid along orthogonal grid plans. Mohenjo-daro had some of the world's earliest urban sanitation, including private bathing rooms, covered street drains, terracotta drain chutes, and public reservoirs like the Great Bath, showing centralized civil engineering centuries ahead of its time.

description: Semitic-speaking workers in the Egyptian turquoise mines adapted simplified Egyptian hieroglyphs to represent single consonants rather than words or syllables, creating the Proto-Sinaitic script. This streamlined system was refined by Phoenician traders and became the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic alphabets.

description: King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 legal judgments inscribed on a diorite stele displayed in public. The code set out rules of evidence, contracts, commercial liability and scaled penalties, including "an eye for an eye", formalizing royal justice over local arbitration across an entire empire.

name: Monumental earthworks of Poverty Point
description: In northeastern Louisiana along Bayou Maçon, Indigenous hunter-gatherer-fishers constructed one of the most astonishing monumental earthwork complexes in North America, moving an estimated 750,000 cubic meters of earth without beasts of burden or wheeled carts. The site features six massive concentric semi-elliptical earthen ridges surrounding a central plaza and dominated by the 22-meter-tall bird-shaped Mound A. A vibrant continental trade hub, Poverty Point imported tons of exotic lithic raw materials—novaculite, galena, quartz crystal, and copper—from across eastern North America, alongside millions of distinctive baked-clay cooking balls known as Poverty Point Objects.

name: Domestication of the chicken
description: Every chicken alive descends from the red junglefowl, a wild bird of Southeast Asia. Genetic studies once put its domestication about 8,000 years ago, but a 2022 reassessment of ancient bones found the oldest known domestic chickens at Ban Non Wat in northeastern Thailand, dated to between 1650 and 1250 BCE. From Southeast Asia chickens were carried across Asia, Africa and Europe, and they are now among the most common domesticated animals in the world.

name: Lapita ocean voyaging
description: Mastering advanced open-ocean navigation, Austronesian-speaking seafaring communities known archaeologically as the Lapita culture embarked on one of the greatest maritime expansions in human history. Navigating across thousands of kilometers of open Pacific waters beyond the sight of land by reading ocean swells, wind patterns, and star paths in double-hulled outrigger canoes, they colonized Remote Oceania from the Bismarck Archipelago through the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, and outward to Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa. Carrying breeding populations of pigs, dogs, chickens, and root crops alongside their unmistakable dentate-stamped red-slipped ceramics, Lapita voyagers laid the ancestral cultural and linguistic foundations of Polynesia and Micronesia.

description: Smiths developed bloomeries and bellows able to reach the temperatures needed to reduce iron ore into workable sponge iron. Because iron ore is far more common than copper and scarce tin, bloomery iron made tools and weapons widely available, supporting expanded farming and large armies.

name: Invasion of the Sea Peoples
description: Around 1200 BCE, at the end of the Late Bronze Age, bands of raiders and migrants later called the Sea Peoples, among them the Sherden, Lukka, Shekelesh, Peleset and Tjekker, attacked Egypt and the coasts of the eastern Mediterranean. Ramesses III recorded on his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu that in his eighth year he defeated them on land and in a great sea battle in the Nile Delta; the reliefs show warriors travelling with women and children in ox-carts. Once blamed for the Bronze Age collapse, in which the Hittite Empire, Mycenaean palaces and cities such as Ugarit fell, they are now more often seen as people displaced by a crisis already under way. The Peleset are generally identified with the Philistines, who settled on the southern Levantine coast.

name: Nok terracotta sculpture and metallurgy
description: On the Jos Plateau of central Nigeria, the Nok culture created sub-Saharan Africa's earliest known monumental figurative art tradition alongside early bloomery iron-smelting technology. Nok artisans sculpted hollow, coiled terracotta human figures and animal effigies remarkable for their expressive stylization, pierced triangular eyes and pupils, elaborate braided hairstyles, and detailed beadwork ornaments. Contemporaneous with their terracotta sculpture, Nok settlements at Taruga operated sophisticated shaft bloomeries, demonstrating the independent or early development of iron metallurgy in West Africa without a preceding bronze age.

name: The ancient Olympic Games
description: In 776 BCE, according to ancient Greek tradition, the first recorded Olympic Games were held at the sacred sanctuary of Olympia in Elis, inaugurating the four-year Olympiad cycle that served as the chronological backbone of the Classical Hellenic world. Instituted under a sacred panhellenic truce that suspended hostilities between warring city-states, the games brought athletes across Greece and its Mediterranean colonies to compete in footraces, the pentathlon, pankration, and chariot racing in honor of Zeus. The Olympic festival fostered a shared Hellenic cultural identity that transcended political fragmentation.

name: Standardized minted coinage
description: The Kingdom of Lydia introduced state-guaranteed coins stamped from electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, bearing a royal lion emblem. By certifying purity and weight with a government mark, coins replaced weighing raw metal at every transaction, laying the groundwork for market economies and money taxation.

name: Qin unification of China
description: In 221 BCE, the state of Qin conquered the last of the Warring States, ending centuries of endemic division and inaugurating the imperial era of China under its first emperor, Qin Shi Huang. The Qin regime imposed sweeping standardization across the realm: establishing a uniform legalist administrative code, standardizing Chinese writing into the Small Seal script, issuing unified round bronze Ban Liang currency, and standardizing weights, measures, and cart axle gauges. Connecting regional defensive walls into the first Great Wall and constructing the colossal Terracotta Army guarding his subterranean mausoleum at Lintong, Qin unification established the institutional and territorial blueprint for two millennia of imperial Chinese statehood.

name: Invention of papermaking
description: Early finds, including the Fangmatan paper map, show that Han Chinese craftspeople were already making paper from plant fibres suspended in water on screens well before 1 CE, long before Cai Lun codified the process in 105 CE. This light, cheap medium replaced bulky bamboo strips and expensive silk, lowering the cost of record-keeping and literacy.

name: Opening of the Silk Road
description: Following the diplomatic missions of Han envoy Zhang Qian to the Western Regions around 130 BCE, the Han dynasty secured the Hexi Corridor and opened regular trans-continental commerce connecting China with Central Asia, Parthia, and the Mediterranean basin. Caravans traversing the treacherous deserts of the Tarim Basin carried Chinese silk, lacquer, cast iron, and paper westward, exchanging them for Central Asian 'Heavenly Horses' from Dayuan, jade from Khotan, alfalfa, grapes, and Roman glassware. Beyond moving commodities, the Silk Road became the preeminent conduit for intercultural exchange across Afro-Eurasia, transmitting artistic styles, technologies, and the spread of Buddhism across Asia.
